newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ruling party faces critical convention.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ruling party faces critical convention.

text.p: President Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) opens a watershed convention on Friday which may decide whether it reforms for the next century or risks losing a 67-year hold on power.

Battered last year by the worst string of election defeats in its history and blamed by voters for massive corruption and Mexico's deepest recession in 60 years, the PRI leadership wants to revamp the party before voters bury it.

"The idea is to transform the party and put it in tune with a new Mexican society," PRI leader Santiago Onate told foreign correspondents recently. "The aim is to overcome what is obsolete (in the PRI)."
Time is short. Mexico holds its first election next year for mayor of Mexico City, a job hitherto held by a presidential appointee, and nationwide elections for congress.

Historically all of Mexico's 30 state governors were PRI men as well as almost all congressmen. But the conservative National Action Party (PAN) now runs four states, has 25 seats in the 128-member Senate and expects further gains next year.
Onate not only has to worry about fighting other parties during the assembly, which starts on Friday evening and ends Sunday at lunchtime. He also faces a strong challenge from within the PRI.

Hardliners who see the party as the eternal government of Mexico are opposed to Onate's proposals to streamline party organisation and reduce the weight of its block representation from unions and peasant groups -- useful for bringing in votes on election day.

Appointed last year by Zedillo to modernise the party, whose roots remained firmly in the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, Onate hoped advance discussion by PRI activists up and down the country of hundreds of detailed proposals would ensure the assembly presents a united front.
But there were signs that was not going to happen.

Fidel Velazquez, Mexico's foremost labour patriarch and a pillar of the PRI for more than half a century, stung Onate this month by publicly lashing the PRI leadership as "pure bureaucrats." Behind him, analysts said, were other hardline groups opposed to change and Onate's leadership of the party.

One often-mentioned name was Manuel Bartlett, governor of the powerful state of Puebla and a former Interior Minister widely accused of engineering the 1988 presidential victory of Carlos Salinas by dubious means. Another was Fernando Gutierrez Barrios, a once all-powerful head of state intelligence who was shunted to the sidelines under Zedillo.

"The PRI is very divided," political analyst Sergio Sarmiento told Reuters. "The group representing Zedillo, which is led by Onate, has very little strength to control the party. Usually in the past when there was disagreement the president (of the Republic) would impose a line. Now it is not so clear. The president has withdrawn from the party."

Zedillo repeatedly said he wanted a "healthy distance" between himself and the PRI, partly because of accusations that past presidents were willing to divert government resources to ensuring PRI election triumphs.

This upset hardliners who saw Zedillo's closeness to the PRI as the best guarantee of continuing its monopoly on government. One member of the old guard, Manuel Garza Gonzalez, said the correct distance between the president and his party was a bearhug.
Not everyone predicted open clashes during the convention.

Jaime Gonzalez Graf, a political scientist, told Reuters the PRI traditionally shunned open conflict in the middle of a presidential term, preferring to save its energy to fight over who should be the presidential candidate in 1999.
"The most controversial topic on the agenda will be the way PRI candidates for elections are picked," he said.
